name: Fall armyworm
description: A moth caterpillar (Spodoptera frugiperda) that feeds in the whorl of young maize and on leaves and cobs. Fresh damage shows as small 'windows' in leaves, ragged holes and sawdust-like droppings in the funnel.

cultural: Scout fields at least twice a week from emergence, checking the whorl of 20 plants in a zig-zag pattern.
Plant early and at the same time as neighbours to reduce staggered infestation.
Intercrop maize with beans or desmodium to reduce egg-laying.
biological: Apply botanical or biological products such as neem-based or Bacillus thuringiensis products registered in Kenya.
Conserve natural enemies such as earwigs, ants and parasitic wasps.
chemical: Use only products registered by the Pest Control Products Board (PCPB) for fall armyworm and follow the label exactly.
Target spraying at the whorl in early morning or late evening and rotate active ingredients.
prevention: Remove crop residues after harvest and plough to expose pupae.
Report new infestations early so neighbours can be warned.

name: Maize stem borer
description: Caterpillars that tunnel into maize stems, causing 'dead hearts' in young plants, small shot-holes in leaves and broken stalks.

cultural: Uproot and destroy plants showing dead hearts.
Practise crop rotation and avoid maize after maize.
Use push-pull (desmodium and Napier grass) where possible.
biological: Encourage parasitoids and predators by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.
chemical: If chemicals are necessary, ask an officer for a PCPB-registered product and apply into the whorl.
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties recommended by KALRO.

name: Maize lethal necrosis (MLN)
description: A viral disease caused by two viruses acting together. Leaves show chlorotic mottling from the base, then drying from the edges; plants may die early and cobs are small or empty.

cultural: Uproot and destroy infected plants early and bury or burn them.
Rotate with non-cereal crops such as beans for at least one season.
Control weeds and volunteer maize that can host the viruses.
biological: No biological cure exists; rely on clean seed and field hygiene.
chemical: Insecticides do not cure the disease; consult an extension officer about managing insect vectors such as thrips.
prevention: Use certified, MLN-tolerant seed from reputable seed companies.
Avoid moving maize residues from infected to clean areas.

name: Late blight
description: A fungus-like disease (Phytophthora infestans) that spreads fast in cool, wet weather. Leaves show dark water-soaked patches, often with white mould underneath; tubers and fruits rot.

cultural: Remove and destroy infected plants and volunteers.
Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead irrigation.
Hill up potatoes to protect tubers.
biological: Use compost and healthy soil practices; copper-based products may be allowed under organic systems.
chemical: Apply a PCPB-registered fungicide before symptoms spread, following the label for interval and protective clothing.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed and resistant varieties.
Rotate crops and avoid planting potato after tomato.

name: Tomato leafminer (Tuta absoluta)
description: A moth whose larvae mine leaves, stems and fruits, leaving blotchy transparent mines and holes in fruit.

cultural: Remove and bury heavily mined leaves and infested fruit.
Use pheromone traps to monitor moth numbers.
Keep the field and greenhouse free of weeds.
biological: Use biopesticides such as Bacillus thuringiensis or neem and conserve predatory bugs.
chemical: Rotate PCPB-registered insecticides with different modes of action to slow resistance.
prevention: Clean up crop residues after harvest.

name: Coffee leaf rust
description: A fungal disease (Hemileia vastatrix) causing yellow-orange powdery spots on the underside of leaves, followed by leaf drop and reduced yield.

cultural: Prune and thin the canopy to improve airflow.
Maintain shade and balanced nutrition to keep trees vigorous.
Remove heavily infected branches.
biological: Copper-based fungicides are commonly used; follow organic standards if applicable.
chemical: Spray a PCPB-registered fungicide at the start of the rains, following label rates and intervals.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties such as Ruiru 11 or Batian where suitable.

name: Banana Xanthomonas wilt
description: A bacterial disease causing yellowing and wilting of leaves, premature ripening and rotting of fruit, and yellow bacterial ooze from cut stems.

cultural: Cut and remove the male bud with a forked stick to stop insect spread.
Disinfect tools with fire, bleach or Jik between plants.
Uproot and destroy infected plants completely.
biological: No biological cure; rely on sanitation.
chemical: There is no effective chemical treatment; contact your county plant health office.
prevention: Use clean planting material from tissue culture.
Do not move suckers from infected farms.

name: Cassava mosaic disease
description: A viral disease spread by whiteflies and infected cuttings. Leaves show pale or yellow mosaic patterns, distortion and stunting.

cultural: Rogue out infected plants early.
Plant only cuttings from healthy plants.
chemical: Insecticides are rarely economic; seek advice from an extension officer.
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties from certified sources.

name: Diamondback moth
description: A small moth whose green larvae feed on the underside of kale and cabbage leaves, leaving small holes and translucent windows.

cultural: Handpick larvae on small plots and remove crop residues.
Use overhead irrigation briefly to dislodge larvae where suitable.
Intercrop with onions, coriander or tomato.
biological: Use Bacillus thuringiensis or neem products and protect parasitic wasps.
chemical: Rotate PCPB-registered insecticides and observe the pre-harvest interval, which is critical for leafy vegetables.
prevention: Avoid continuous planting of brassicas in the same field.

name: Aphids
description: Small sap-sucking insects that cluster on young shoots and leaf undersides, causing curling, stunting, sticky honeydew and sooty mould.

cultural: Check shoot tips weekly and wash off small colonies with water or soapy water.
Control ants that protect aphids.
biological: Encourage ladybirds and lacewings; use neem or soap sprays.
chemical: Only if populations are high, use a PCPB-registered product and avoid spraying during flowering to protect bees.
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser, which encourages soft growth.

name: Bean rust
description: A fungal disease producing small reddish-brown pustules on bean leaves that release powdery spores and cause early leaf drop.

cultural: Rotate beans with cereals.
Space plants for airflow and avoid working in wet fields.
biological: Use resistant varieties as the main control.
chemical: If severe, apply a registered fungicide as directed on the label.
prevention: Destroy residues after harvest and use certified seed.
